It goes without saying that data breaches and data leaks are getting more brazen in today’s cybersecurity landscape.

Whether it’s done by an attacker, by someone inside an organization, or as the result of problematic data security practices, data leaks and breaches require individuals to be the last line of defense against bad actors.
Let’s discuss some of the ways in which users online can increase their security or better respond to a cybersecurity incident of this sort.

Data breaches in cybersecurity refer to incidents where sensitive or personal information is accessed, taken (either by theft, copying, or transmission of the information) or viewed by a party that shouldn’t have access to that information.

Data breaches can potentially be the outcome of a cyberattack, an unintentional fault by an employee or an oversight in cybersecurity practices, or perhaps occur due to flaws and vulnerabilities in cybersecurity infrastructure.

Data leakage, meanwhile, occurs when sensitive or confidential information gets exposed in error. A system could have been left open by mistake, data could have been shared wrongly, or data potentially stored somewhere it shouldn’t have been.

With the prevalence of artificial intelligence, attacks or exploitations of flaws and vulnerabilities in programs are growing more common, with these attacks also ramping up in scale. Both data breaches and data leaks can occur separately or in tandem, in any case.
Oftentimes, it’s not a matter of if your information will figure in a data breach or data leak, but rather a question of when it’ll happen, and what you will do as a counter.
It is commonly the responsibility of companies to inform authorities of these cybersecurity incidents.

For instance, the Philippines has a data privacy law requiring timely disclosures of such attacks or leaks occurring. However, this requires time to do investigations into the nature of attacks to determine if an attack actually happened and if data was actually leaked or taken.
As such, sometimes the rumor or report of a data breach or leak can be enough to spur security-minded people into action.

After a report of a data breach or leak, it is good practice to be proactive in protecting your data. There are some things that are out of the scope of basic cybersecurity measures, but there’s still plenty for a lay person to do when that report comes in.

It’s recommended that you first find out how bad the problem is. One of the most important things to account for is the extent of the problem. Depending on what was leaked, you’ll need to do different things to mitigate and protect yourself. Once a data breach or leak is reported, find out what information was taken, then you can begin the work.
For the average internet user, there are a number of different types of information to consider:

items: Personal data, or personal identifiable information (PII): Names, contact details, national ID numbers, or even your address.
Financial information: Bank accounts, credit card information, and payment records
Credential information: This includes usernames, passwords, and tokens or API keys.
Medical information: Aside from health records, these can include things like the diagnoses, details of your prescriptions, and insurance information.

blocks.text: First, change your passwords. Leaked PIIs and credential information can be taken advantage of by attackers. They can use automated tools to test what available PIIs and credentials they might have taken against multiple sites and services — they can even do this at scale with AI now.

To counter this, make sure all your passwords are different, and change the passwords of any affected site and service alongside sites and services sharing the same or similar passwords to one that figured in a data breach. It’s also recommended to use an offline password manager to store your passwords under a central super-password to keep things in order.

Second, enable two-factor authentication where applicable. As the Philippines is the ASEAN country most willing to tolerate and accept friction to maintain security and prevent scams, it goes without saying that you should have two-factor authentication where applicable.

Third, monitor your accounts for suspicious activity. Knowing your data is out there means being more alert to bad actors who’ve already taken advantage of your data that’s circling around the dark places on the internet.

blocks.caption: Scams from false claims: How to spot them

blocks.text: Lastly, you are already a target, so act like one. If you know your data is out there, and scams and bad actors are out there itching to get at your money or other important data, it may be safer to act with prudence. Never click unverified links in messages. Assume that phishing emails, texts, or phone calls will use your personal data to try and entice you to let your guard down, so confirm any calls, emails, or offers you get with the official people sending them.

As the last line of defense, you have a say in how to respond to reports of data breaches or leaks. You may be the victim of a data breach or a leak, but that doesn’t mean you have to remain a victim to scammers and other bad actors. – Rappler.com
